title: Command of Evidence, Part 1: The Method and Two Questions

beats.say: Command of evidence questions give you a claim, and ask which piece of evidence relates to it. Your job is to match the evidence to the exact claim.

card.text: Match the evidence to the claim

beats.say: There are two kinds. Textual evidence asks which finding would support or weaken a hypothesis, or which quotation illustrates a claim about a character.
Quantitative evidence gives you a table or a graph, and asks which choice uses the data to support a claim.
Step one. Find the exact claim. It is often in the last sentence of the text, such as the researchers hypothesized that, or the narrator portrays.
Step two. Turn the claim into a prediction. Finish this sentence in your head: if this is true, we should see what?
beats.item: Predict: if true, we should see ___

beats.say: Step three. For a table, read the column headers and the units before you read the choices.
Step four. Eliminate anything inaccurate, then anything irrelevant to the claim. The survivor is the answer.

scenes.title: What the answer must do
rows: show it failing, or another cause
be accurate and match the claim

beats.say: To support a hypothesis, the answer must show the predicted result happening, in the group the hypothesis is about.
To weaken a claim, the answer must show the predicted result not happening, or offer another explanation.
To illustrate a portrayal, a quotation must show every trait that the claim names, not just one of them.
With data, a choice must be accurate according to the table, and also match the comparison made in the claim.
Easy question. We read a short hypothesis, and then pick the finding that would most directly support it. First we turn the hypothesis into a prediction.

scenes.title: Read the text
scenes.text: A biologist hypothesized that a species of desert beetle collects drinking water from morning fog, which condenses on the bumps of its shell.

beats.say: The claim is that the beetle gets its drinking water from fog. Notice that fog is the key part.
Our prediction is, if fog gives the beetles water, then beetles without fog should end up drier.

scenes.title: Which finding supports the hypothesis?
scenes.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the biologist's hypothesis?

options.A: The beetles are most active in the late afternoon.
options.B: Beetles kept without fog lost more body water than beetles kept with fog.
options.C: The beetles' shells are darker than the sand around them.
options.D: Other desert insects also have bumps on their shells.

beats.say: Choice A is about when the beetles are active. It says nothing about water, so it is irrelevant.
Choice C is about the color of the shell. Color has nothing to do with fog, so it does not test the hypothesis.
Choice D is about other insects. The hypothesis is about this species, so this is the wrong group.
Choice B compares fog with no fog, and shows the predicted difference. The answer is B.
Medium question. Now a table. Every wrong choice may be true, so we check two things: is it accurate, and does it connect to the claim?

scenes.title: Riders per day on three streets

beats.say: A planner claims that new bike lanes on Harlow Street increased cycling there, while nearby streets without lanes stayed about the same.
Penn Street had no new lanes, and its riders went from two hundred eighty to two hundred ninety. That is almost the same.
Doyle Street also had no new lanes, and went from one hundred fifty to one hundred sixty. The claim has two parts, so we need both.

scenes.title: Which choice supports the claim?
scenes.question: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the planner's claim?

options.A: Harlow Street had more riders per day in 2023 than any other street.
options.B: Harlow riders nearly doubled, while Penn and Doyle each gained only ten.
options.C: Doyle Street had the fewest riders per day in both years.
options.D: Penn Street had two hundred eighty riders per day in 2021.

beats.say: Choice D is accurate, but it only gives one number. It says nothing about change, so it is irrelevant.
Choice C is accurate too, but it is about the ranking of Doyle Street, not about the claim.
Choice A is accurate, but it only shows that Harlow is the largest. It does not show growth, or that the other streets stayed flat.
Choice B covers both parts of the claim with correct numbers. Harlow went from three hundred ten to five hundred ninety, and each other street gained ten. The answer is B.
To recap. Find the exact claim, and turn it into a prediction before you read the choices.
Cross out the inaccurate choices, then the choices that are accurate but irrelevant. The survivor matches every part of the claim.
